paper_title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.

Introduction Frontier multimodal models can now control robots directly without task-specific training. For example, GPT-6 Astra runs behind an API with frozen weights and still controls robot zero-shot from images through pose interface [27, 43]. Much of this progress comes from the harness that wraps the frozen model and provides semantic action units [5], virtual camera views [32], agent-written tools and code [13, 17], or low-level VLA skills [44]. However, existing harnesses mainly help the model see and move. Beyond seeing and moving, many manipulation tasks in the physical world depend on contact forces that images cannot show. For example, driving screw requires pressing down while turning until the thread engages, and sorting identical-looking bottles requires comparing their weight. Existing work brings force into such tasks mainly through learning. Specifically, force-aware policies [15, 18, 39] and benchmarks [14] add wrist force as network input to visuomotor policies [6] and vision-language-action (VLA) models [24]. However, this approach requires demonstrations for every task and updates model weights, so it cannot be applied to an API-only frozen model. Meanwhile, existing harnesses for frozen models that expose contact typically pass raw wrench and tactile values [7, 29] or ask the model to generate force-control code [4, 28]. Yet these designs still leave the model to parse raw sensor numbers or write low-level control without calibrated physical feedback. We therefore ask: can frozen frontier model understand force and use it to complete manipulation tasks that cannot be done without it? Answering this question raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model through general skills that regulate force on their own under the models direction. Second, frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams or choose actions from raw numbers alone, so the system must return force in form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, harness that lets frozen frontier model use wrist force without demonstrations or training. As shown in Figure 1, ForceHarness places three layers between the model and the robot. At the bottom, force sensing and calibration layer estimates hand force from wrist sensor or joint torques alone and removes sensor offsets. In the middle, self-terminating force primitives address the first challenge by turning common contact skills such as guarded moves, sliding, and insertion into callable tools. Once called, each primitive regulates force on its own and returns at contact event. At the top, physics translation layer addresses the second challenge by converting each primitives force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty estimates and status flags, such as payload mass, contact height, and friction. At each turn, the model calls primitive, reads the returned physical quantities, and decides what to do next. Together, these three layers form general set of building blocks that bridges frozen frontier model and low-level force control. We evaluate ForceHarness on real robot arm without wrist force sensor and across two simulation benchmarks, as summarized in Figure 1. On the real robot, we design six contact-rich tasks and find that ForceHarness raises the zeroshot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% without force to 90.0%. In simulation, the same model with ForceHarness operates from RGB images on the public ForceBench suite [14] and improves from 70.0% to 87.5%, surpassing the force-aware policies trained on that benchmark. To further compare frozen models with classical controllers and learned force policies under identical conditions, we build HiddenPhys, seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On HiddenPhys, ForceHarness raises the success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 62.1% to 96.4%, matching hand-written expert force controllers and far exceeding Diffusion Policy [6], π0.5 [24], and ForceVLA [39] trained on about 200 demonstrations per task. Our contributions are: We propose ForceHarness, three-layer harness of force calibration, self-terminating force primitives, and physics translation that bridges an API-only frozen model and low-level force control without demonstrations or training. We build HiddenPhys, seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables that includes expert force controllers and learned force policies evaluated on identical seeds. Experiments on real robot and two simulated benchmarks show that ForceHarness lets frozen frontier models make full use of force for contact-rich manipulation, outperforming both training-based methods and the same harness without force. 2. Related work Harness for embodied AI. GPT-6 Astra showed that frozen frontier model, given images and pose interface, can act as zero-shot robot policy [43], and systematic evaluations have mapped what such models can and cannot do as embodied policies [11, 27]. Following Code as Policies [20], in which language model writes robot programs over control primitives, the harness around the frozen model has become design variable of its own. Some harnesses change how the model acts, through semantic action units [5], task-agnostic agent harness [31], agent-written tools [13], or code that runs with no model in the loop [17]. Others change what it perceives, through calibrated perception tools [19] or rendered virtual views [32]. Others add memory of demonstrations and past interaction [21], orchestrate learned policies as skills [10, 44], or let second agent revise the harness itself [30, 36]. However, few of these harnesses consider force: most have no force channel, and the rest mainly pass raw readings or force cap to the agent [79, 37]. ForceHarness is instead built around force: it regulates force beneath the model and reports it to the model as physical quantities. 2 Force for embodied AI. Force has been central to manipulation since hybrid position/force control [26] and impedance control [16], and force-torque measurements can identify payload [1] or locate contact [2], but such methods are engineered task by task. Learned policies instead take force as network input [12, 15, 18, 23, 33, 39], and ForceBench [14] compares integration designs on π0.5; all of them require demonstrations or simulated training, and weight updates. Language models have also used force at inference time by reading sensed properties as sentences [45], generating code with force feedback [4, 22], tuning the impedance of base policy [40, 41], or choosing recovery actions above trained skill [25]. Recent studies give GPT-6 Astra tactile or force readings directly [29, 34, 35, 38, 46], and FORCA [28] has coding agent write force-feedback programs and revise them between rollouts. ForceHarness differs in bringing control and perception of force together with no training: primitives regulate force beneath the model, and the model reads calibrated physical quantities after each one. 3. Method 3.1. Overview ForceHarness sits between frozen model and robot and has three layers, shown in Figure 2. The bottom layer, force sensing and calibration, turns the robots raw signals into calibrated estimate of the force that the environment applies to the hand. The middle layer is menu of self-terminating force primitives, contact skills that regulate force on their own and stop at contact event. The top layer, the physics translation layer, converts the force trace of each primitive into physical quantities with uncertainties. Because the model is reached only through an API and needs seconds for each decision, force enters the loop twice. Inside primitive it controls contact at the rate of the controller, and in the tool result it informs the models next decision. None of the layers assumes particular arm, and Sec. of the supplementary material lists the constants of each robot and simulator. 3.2. The layer therefore controls when it reads rather than how it filters. It tares at rest, re-zeroing before each empty-hand primitive so that the zero is taken close to the pose of the coming contact. After each primitive it lets the arm settle, then reads, relaxing the controller onto the measured pose and averaging the force over short still window. Finally, it reports changes, giving each still reading relative to reference from the same episode, such as the empty hand or the moment of the grasp, so that the model compares readings instead of trusting absolute values. In simulation, the wrist sensor is instead zeroed at reset and after reorienting the tool. 3.3. Physics translation layer frozen model has not learned to read raw force, and the hundreds of samples that primitive logs give it little basis for its next decision. The top layer therefore translates each force trace into few physical quantities, the numbers person would read off the trace, and returns them as the tool result. Its estimators are deliberately simple and fixed, built only from averages and least-squares fits with propagated errors. Every quantity follows the recipe shown as strip in Figure 2. The layer removes the zero and any held load, keeps only the window in which the quantity has single meaning, and reports the value with its uncertainty σ and with flags that warn, for instance, of lost contact. At every turn the model reads the instruction, the tool menu, the call history, and the latest observations, and it answers with one tool call. Instructions are written by hand for each task and never reveal the hidden variables of an episode. task usually starts without force, as the model points at target in the image, locate turns that pixel into 3D point from depth, and position moves bring the hand close. The model then switches to force primitives and sets their parameters from what it has seen and read so far. Each primitive stops on its own, and its force comes back translated into physical quantities as the tool result. From these quantities the model judges what happened, for example whether part has seated or needs another attempt, and it chooses the next call until it ends the episode. Calibration and safety stay beneath the model, because the bottom layer keeps the force zeroed by the rules of Sec. 3.2 and the fixed guard limits force, speed, and workspace for every primitive whatever the model asks. 4. The HiddenPhys benchmark Public force benchmarks such as ForceBench [14] are built to train and compare learned policies. We complement them with HiddenPhys, benchmark of seven manipulation tasks in robosuite on MuJoCo. Its tasks come from real-world contact scenarios and add fine manipulation that ForceBench does not cover. 5 Table 2. The seven tasks of HiddenPhys. Each task hides one physical variable that decides success, as listed in Table 2. In Weight and CoM the robot must judge load that it is holding, and in Wipe and Stack it must find surface whose height is uncertain. Peg asks it to find hole by touch, while Latch and Lock ask it to operate mechanism without damaging it. The instruction states the range of the hidden variable but never its value, which is drawn from the episode seed, so every method faces the same episodes. Setting and references. Panda arm runs operationalspace control, and force is the wrist sensor reading with added noise and per-episode bias. To isolate force from visual perception, frozen model reads object poses as noisy text instead of images, while the real robot and ForceBench cover camera input. HiddenPhys ships with three kinds of reference. The expert force controller is hand-written state machine for each task, and the position-only controller makes the same motions without using force. The learned policies are Diffusion Policy [6] and π0.5 [24], each trained with and without force input, together with controlled multi-task variant of ForceVLA [39], and all of them learn from about 200 expert demonstrations per task. Besides success, HiddenPhys counts damage, an episode in which the force on handle passes its damage threshold. Sec. of the supplementary material gives the task cards, success checks, and seeds, and Sec. gives the training recipes. 5. Experiments We evaluate ForceHarness on real robot, on the public ForceBench suite, and on HiddenPhys, shown in Figure 3. In each setting, the same frozen model runs with ForceHarness and with no-force control, which keeps the harness and its safety limits but removes force primitives and force readings. 5.1. In Table 3, ForceHarness raises GPT-6 Astra from 2/60 without force to 54/60 across all six tasks, while GPT6.1 Sol reaches 47/60 under the same prompts. On bottle sorting and telling soft from hard, RGB-D images give no cue to mass or stiffness, leaving the no-force control at 0/10 on both. On the sensorless FR3, joint-torque estimates drift with arm pose and misstate absolute grams, yet taring at rest, settling before reading, and comparing within-episode changes keep relative order reliable. This lets Astra score 10/10 on both tasks and Sol score 8/10 and 10/10, even when no probing method is given for soft versus hard. On the four contact tasks, wrist depth localizes targets only to about 1 to 2 cm, so position-only steps either miss the surface or hit the collision guard without knowing the contact load, succeeding in only 2 of 40 episodes. With ForceHarness, force acts both inside and between primitives, as Figure 1 illustrates. Inside each call, guarded moves and admittance control absorb height and pose error, holding steady contact across the flat board or curved eggplant and spiraling at 1 until resistance drop guides the USB plug into its port. Between calls, tool results and images guide adaptation: remaining ink after an 8 wipe prompts Astra to retry at 10 N, rising side load during screwing triggers an inplace release before binding, and 2.77 mean force over 51 mm peel tells Astra to keep its 6 target. Calibrated jointtorque sensing, self-terminating primitives, and physical quantities thus make zero-shot contact manipulation reliable without wrist sensor. 5.2. ForceBench Experimental setting. Force estimate. Polymetis forwards the filtered external joint torques that libfranka estimates but not wrench, so the guard solves Eq. 1 of the main paper on every tick by least squares with the flange Jacobian of the controllers own kinematic model. It also checks the joint torque that no flange wrench explains, and residual above 3 Nm or Jacobian near singularity ends the episode with fault. The estimate has little noise, 0.03 to 0.05 at rest, but its zero shifts by few newtons with the approach direction, joint friction in motion, and the wrist angle. Filtering cannot remove such an offset, so we calibrate only the offset and read force by the three rules of Sec. 3.2 of the main paper. The harness tares with the gripper open before each empty-hand primitive, and after every primitive it relaxes the target onto the measured pose for 0.8 and then averages the wrench over 0.5 s. Relaxing lowers the median difference between consecutive still readings from 1.07 to 0.08 over 999 empty-hand windows, because target that leads the joints pushes against joint friction, which the estimate reports as external force. Each still reading is reported relative to the same reading at the start of the episode, and with an object in the hand also as the change since the grasp. Lifted weights are therefore compared within an episode rather than read in grams. Safety. Beneath the guard of Sec.
